justification: All three provided articles concern CTRL (chymotrypsin-like protease) in the context of pancreatic digestive enzyme biology, trypsinogen degradation, and chronic/acute pancreatitis in humans and mouse models. None of them mention inguinal, femoral, or abdominal hernia, nor any connective tissue, collagen, or abdominal wall integrity phenotype that could serve as a mechanistic bridge. There is no genetic association, expression, pathway, or animal model evidence linking CTRL to hernia in this literature set. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a negligible allowance for indirect biological speculation.

All provided articles concern biallelic loss-of-function ZNF699 variants causing DEGCAGS syndrome, a rare recessive multisystem developmental disorder; none report neutrophil percentage, quantitative blood-count traits, or GWAS/association data for this hematologic index. The closest relevant item is a single case report of syndromic combined immunodeficiency with severe B-cell depletion (PMID 42534679), which suggests hematopoietic/immune involvement and provides weak biological plausibility for altered leukocyte subsets, but it describes lymphoid rather than neutrophil abnormalities and is a single proband. No study demonstrates variants in ZNF699 associated with neutrophil percentage in humans, so Established is essentially excluded and Existing is only marginally supported by the immune/hematologic phenotype. The bulk of the probability therefore falls on Novel, with a substantial share to Hypothesized given the immunologic findings and the gene's role as a KRAB zinc-finger transcriptional regulator of unknown function.

None of the provided articles mention heart failure or any cardiac phenotype. The SIGLEC15 literature here concerns osteoclast differentiation and bone remodeling (mouse knockouts, in vitro studies), immune checkpoint biology in cancer, Siglec family evolution, and one exome-wide association with tuberculosis susceptibility. There is no genetic variant evidence, expression data, or mechanistic pathway linking SIGLEC15 to heart failure in humans or animal models. The only human genetic study (PMID 30898644) concerns tuberculosis, which is unrelated to heart failure. Therefore the gene–phenotype relationship is best classified as Novel.

phenotype: Benign and in situ intestinal neoplasms
justification: None of the provided articles address benign or in situ intestinal neoplasms. ABHD16A literature concerns lysophosphatidylserine metabolism (PMIDs 25580854, 32462874), complex hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic variants (PMIDs 34866177, 34587489, 34489854, 41561502), antiviral IFITM1 depalmitoylation (PMIDs 40434075, 39601593), mitochondrial fission/fusion (PMID 36448541), chickenpox susceptibility (PMID 36620086), and pig back fat thickness (PMID 22367074). There is no report of tumor initiation, adenoma, polyps, or intestinal epithelial neoplastic transformation involving ABHD16A, nor any plausible directly relevant oncogenic pathway described here. A tiny residual probability is assigned to "hypothesized" only because lipid signaling and immune modulation are broadly relevant to tumorigenesis, but this is speculative and not supported by any of the cited work.

ot_trait: Female infertility due to fertilization defect
justification: The strongest paper (PMID 32923640) states that human GWAS have linked SNPs in NEMP1 to early menopause—a well-recognized precursor/risk factor for female infertility—which would support "Existing"; however, that association is cited as background, while the paper's own results are entirely from Drosophila, C. elegans, zebrafish, and mouse knockouts showing sterility/early loss of fertility and germline nuclear envelope defects. The other papers (PMIDs 36215313, 34133414) address erythropoiesis and nuclear lipid droplets in mice and worms, providing no human variant data. Thus there are no articles here reporting NEMP1 variants in human probands or families with infertility, ruling out "Established." The evidence in this set is dominated by strong, mechanistically relevant animal-model data, favoring "Hypothesized," with substantial weight on "Existing" because of the cited human GWAS link to early menopause.

phenotype: Lymphocytes/100 leukocytes in Blood by Automated count
justification: None of the provided articles report a human genetic association between DCTD variants and lymphocyte percentage or any blood-count trait; the human variant studies involving DCTD concern hepatocellular carcinoma survival and gemcitabine response/toxicity (PMIDs 42512318, 20028759, 26372358), which are unrelated phenotypes. The strongest biologically relevant evidence is a genome-wide CRISPR activation screen in mouse embryonic stem cells in which Dctd was one of seven genes whose activation induced hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells with multilineage output including T and B lymphoid engraftment (PMID 40209065) — a plausible mechanistic link to lymphocyte production, but in mouse/in vitro, thus supporting "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing." Other papers address DCTD's role in dNTP pool balance, mutagenesis, and mitochondrial DNA depletion (PMIDs 24362886, 31351931, 7642519), which are general proliferative/nucleotide-metabolism functions that could indirectly bear on hematopoiesis but provide no direct phenotype evidence. Given the mouse hematopoietic evidence, a fully "Novel" designation is less likely but remains plausible since the connection to lymphocyte fraction specifically is indirect.

None of the provided articles examine body weight, obesity, BMI, or any anthropometric trait in relation to TCEA3. The literature concerns TCEA3 as a transcription elongation factor regulated by USP47, tRF-Leu-CAG, and linc01105/miR-650 in colorectal, lung, and gastric cancers (PMIDs 34630087, 39198937, 40493903), plus its expression in hESC-derived cardiomyocytes and embryonic cardiac structures (PMID 19658189). No human genetic variant studies link TCEA3 to weight, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. A small allowance for Hypothesized reflects generic biological plausibility (roles in apoptosis, differentiation, and cardiac/muscle development that could tangentially relate to growth), but there is no direct mechanistic link to weight regulation, making Novel the most appropriate classification.

phenotype: Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary sarcoidosis
justification: The only provided article is a crosslinking mass spectrometry study of histone/nucleosome protein interactions in human nuclei, which mentions USF3 solely as a nucleosome-interacting protein (PMID: 30021884). It contains no reference to interstitial lung disease, sarcoidosis, pulmonary phenotypes, patients, or genetic variants. There is therefore no evidence in this literature set of any genetic association, functional pathway link, or animal model connecting USF3 to interstitial lung disease or pulmonary sarcoidosis. The co-mention is incidental (the gene appears alone, with no phenotype context), so the relationship should be considered Novel, with a small allowance for hypothesized biology (chromatin/transcription regulation) not documented here.

None of the provided articles measure aspartate aminotransferase or any liver enzyme/hepatic phenotype in relation to ADRA1A. The strongest metabolic evidence concerns metabolic syndrome components (PMIDs 21519279, 22037178, 24249923), which is only indirectly and weakly related to serum AST via fatty liver, and these studies do not report transaminase outcomes. Remaining papers concern schizophrenia, hypertension, vasoconstriction, antipsychotic side effects, anxiety, syncope, and lung cancer—all unrelated to AST levels. There is thus no direct human genetic evidence, and at best a tenuous biological/pathway rationale through adrenergic regulation of metabolism, so the association is essentially novel with a modest possibility of being considered hypothesized.

nearest_curated_disease: CONGENITAL FIBROSIS OF EXTRAOCULAR MUSCLES 5; CFEOM5
justification: None of the provided articles address venous thromboembolism (VTE) in any form. The COL25A1 literature centers on Alzheimer's disease amyloid plaque biology (PMIDs 18501477, 19548013, 33287899), intramuscular motor innervation (PMIDs 24453327, 31875546), and recessive human phenotypes such as congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders, congenital ptosis, and arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (PMIDs 25500261, 26486031, 35077597, 40158061). The only vaguely vascular mention is a review noting COL25A1 can produce vascular Ehlers-Danlos-like features (PMID 36503916), but vEDS involves arterial/hollow organ rupture rather than venous thrombosis, providing at most a tenuous connective-tissue rationale rather than evidence of a VTE link. No human genetic association, no animal model, and no mechanistic pathway connecting COL25A1 to thrombosis is presented, so the relationship is best described as Novel.

phenotype: Specific developmental disorders of scholastic skills
justification: Multiple independent human studies report pathogenic ZC4H2 point mutations in unrelated probands/families with a syndromic X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder featuring intellectual disability and developmental/learning impairment: the original multi-family cohort with missense/nonsense variants (PMID 23623388), the XLID re-sequencing families with p.L66H, p.R18K, p.R213W (PMID 26056227), a large cohort of 23 newly identified families with de novo deleterious variants (PMID 31206972), a Japanese sibship with K209N (PMID 29803542), and additional single-family reports (PMIDs 31885220, 40276104, 36250278). These are sequence-level variants (not merely multigene deletions), replicated across independent families, supporting causality for the cognitive/learning-impairment phenotype. Uncertainty remains because the queried phenotype, "specific developmental disorders of scholastic skills," is nosologically distinct from the global intellectual disability/developmental delay documented in ZARD, so some points are reserved for Existing (ID as a closely related/overlapping mapped phenotype). Animal and in vitro work (zebrafish, mouse knockouts, PMIDs 40632560, 36140726) supports biology but does not by itself establish the human link.

None of the provided articles report a human genetic association between CPNE4 variants and HDL cholesterol or any lipid trait. The human study present (PMID 23202439) concerns CNV deletions in CPNE4 and age at onset of Alzheimer's disease, unrelated to HDL and involving copy number events. The remaining evidence is entirely non-human: chicken muscle glycogen (PMID 32366026), buffalo fertility (PMID 37184817), cattle dry days (PMID 36918047), mouse hearing loss (PMIDs 38915500, 40399499), and mouse hippocampal expression (PMID 33328525). Only the Meigu Yanying chicken study (PMID 41751003) touches a cholesterol-related trait (leg muscle total cholesterol content in poultry), which is neither HDL-specific nor human, giving at most a weak hypothetical metabolic link. Overall the co-mentions are incidental, supporting a largely Novel classification with some allowance for a speculative metabolic/lipid biology link.

None of the supplied articles mention varicose veins, venous insufficiency, vascular biology, or any related phenotype. All papers concern MICAL-L1's cell-biological role in tubular recycling endosome biogenesis, membrane tubulation, cargo delivery, EHD1/Rab35/syndapin2 interactions, and p53-mediated transcriptional regulation in colorectal cancer (PMIDs 30659120, 34100897, 23596323, 25875965, 23572513, 28714518). No human genetic variant data or clinical association with varicose veins are reported, so Established and Existing cannot be supported. A small allowance for Hypothesized is given because endosomal recycling and membrane trafficking could conceivably touch on endothelial/vascular remodeling, but nothing in these abstracts makes that link explicit.

None of the provided articles addresses hip replacement, hip osteoarthritis, joint degeneration, or any musculoskeletal phenotype. The RASSF8 literature here concerns tumour suppressor biology, adherens junction and exocyst-mediated trafficking in Drosophila wing and eye epithelia, border cell migration, and epigenetic regulation in breast cancer. The only human genetic studies mentioning RASSF8 involve an intergenic variant near RASSF8 associated with urinary VEGF (PMID 24876117) and a suggestive, non-genome-wide-significant SNP for sensitive skin (PMID 39598151) — neither is a precursor or risk factor for hip replacement. There is thus no direct or indirect biological rationale linking RASSF8 variants to hip arthroplasty, making this relationship novel, with only a small allowance for generic cell-adhesion/morphogenesis biology that could be argued as hypothetically relevant to joint tissue.

nearest_curated_disease: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH PAROXYSMAL DYSKINESIA OR SEIZURES; IDDPADS
justification: None of the retrieved articles report variants in PDE2A in patients with nonrheumatic valve disease; human genetic evidence for PDE2A concerns early-onset chorea/paroxysmal dyskinesia (PMIDs 29392776, 32467598), primary aldosteronism/bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (PMIDs 33112806, 35813615), congenital scoliosis (PMID 36267860), and impulse control disorders (PMID 32793093) — none a recognized precursor or subtype of valvular heart disease. The only cardiovascular-relevant material is general cAMP/cGMP compartmentation biology in myocardium and endothelium (PMIDs 38776406, 26095046, 15650061, 15769620), which is myocardial/endothelial rather than valvular, providing at best a weak, indirect biological rationale. There is therefore no basis for Established or Existing, and only a thin case for Hypothesized based on cardiac/endothelial cyclic nucleotide signaling. The bulk of probability falls on Novel, with a moderate allocation to Hypothesized given PDE2A's documented cardiovascular expression and function.

None of the provided articles report any association between CKAP4 variants (or CKAP4 biology) and platelet count, function, or platelet-related disorders. The literature covers CKAP4 as a DKK1 receptor in cancer (PMIDs 39689859, 37057110, 39704929), ER sheet morphology (37039099), cardiac fibroblast activation (29386203), podocyte/diabetic kidney disease (40493405, 41316993), and muscle atrophy (39571512). The only hematology-adjacent mention is the TMEM147 study (36044892), where CKAP4 upregulation is a downstream cellular consequence and the blood phenotype is a neutrophil anomaly (pseudo-Pelger-Huët), not platelets. There are no human genetic variant studies in probands, families, or cohorts linking CKAP4 to platelet traits, so Established and Existing are not supportable; a small allowance for Hypothesized is given only because CKAP4 is a broadly expressed cytoskeleton/ER protein whose biology could conceivably touch megakaryocyte/platelet function, though no such evidence appears here.

All human studies listed concern TMC1 variants and non-syndromic/syndromic hearing loss (e.g., PMIDs 34523024, 38066485, 36568409), with no measurement or association with human stature/height. The only "height"-adjacent content is stereocilia length/height regulation in mouse Tmc1/Tmc2 knockout hair cells (PMID 31902726), which refers to actin-core dimensions of hair-cell stereocilia rather than body height, and a C. elegans microgravity study where body length changes were attributed to MEC-4, with tmc-1 downregulation only correlative and non-human (PMID 42300093). No human proband, family, or cohort evidence links TMC1 variants to height, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded. A small amount of weight is retained for "Hypothesized" only because of the loose, non-human "stereocilia height/body length" mechanistic co-mentions, which are not truly relevant to human stature.

phenotype: Monocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
justification: The Japanese BioBank GWAS (PMID 21738478) identified CDK6 as a genome-wide significant locus for a white blood cell subtype count (neutrophils) with pleiotropic effects across WBC subtypes, but the monocyte-count loci reported there were ITGA4, MLZE, STXBP6, and MHC, not CDK6. A human functional/genetic study of the CDK6 variant rs445 (PMID 34116212) reports that this variant lowers myeloid cell levels including granulocytes and alters drug-induced apoptosis in CD11b+ cells, supporting a human variant-level effect on myeloid blood cell counts. The Sardinian GWAS (PMID 36136759) reports two independent CDK6 signals for white-cell morphological parameters measured across populations including monocytes, again in humans, though for morphology rather than absolute counts. Thus there is credible human genetic evidence linking CDK6 to closely related myeloid/leukocyte traits, but no cited study in this list demonstrates replicated association specifically with automated monocyte count, precluding "Established." Remaining articles are cancer/cell-cycle biology and support only mechanistic plausibility (CDK6 as a regulator of hematopoietic and myeloid proliferation).

Neither provided article addresses triglycerides or lipid traits. PMID 36344539 lists EDRF1 as a candidate gene among many for intellectual disability in consanguineous families, with no lipid phenotype. PMID 34827754 identifies EDRF1 as a hub gene in hypoxia/reoxygenation transcriptome networks in a fish species, which is non-human and unrelated to triglyceride metabolism. There is no human genetic association, no functional lipid-related biology, and only incidental co-mention, so the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for indirect metabolic/hypoxia-related pathway speculation.

None of the provided articles addresses stroke, cerebrovascular disease, or any recognized stroke precursor (e.g., atrial fibrillation, hypertension, small-vessel disease) in relation to SNX1. The literature centers on SNX1 as a sorting nexin in retromer/retriever-mediated endosomal trafficking, with genetic association reported only for Alzheimer's disease neuropathology and related neurodegeneration (PMIDs 22673115, 39417691, 39778705) and functional/mechanistic work in Parkinson's models, C. elegans, plants, and cell lines. One paper links SNX proteins to ENaC trafficking and salt/water homeostasis (PMID 40952999), which could weakly touch blood-pressure biology and thus provides a thin hypothetical mechanistic thread, but no stroke phenotype is measured and SNX1 is not the key cargo adaptor identified. There are no human genetic studies reporting SNX1 variants in stroke probands or families, so Established is excluded and Existing is essentially unsupported.

All CLDN14 literature here concerns autosomal recessive non-syndromic deafness (DFNB29), cochlear tight junctions, and renal paracellular calcium/magnesium handling; none reports retinal detachment or retinal breaks. The only ocular mentions are incidental: Cldn14-/- mice serve as deaf controls in a study whose retinal findings pertain to CaV1.3 channels (PMID 19664321), and ocular abnormalities in FHHNC are attributed to CLDN19, not CLDN14 (PMID 26613020). No human genetic study links CLDN14 variants to retinal detachment or any recognized precursor (e.g., high myopia, vitreoretinopathy). There is likewise no functional or expression evidence implicating claudin-14 in retinal adhesion or the retinal pigment epithelium barrier, leaving only a very weak generic tight-junction rationale.

No articles were provided linking RBM12B to hip circumference or any related anthropometric trait. RBM12B is a poorly characterized RNA-binding motif protein gene with no documented functional role in adiposity or body fat distribution in the supplied literature. Without any human genetic association studies, functional data, or animal models, there is no basis for even a hypothesized relationship. A small residual probability is retained because anthropometric GWAS are highly polygenic and such loci are frequently reported in large consortium analyses that may not be captured here.

The single provided article concerns a backward-speech trait and working memory, identifying an incidental novel coding variant in ZBED5 alongside RIC3 and RIPK1; it makes no mention of blood glucose, glycemic traits, or metabolic phenotypes. No study in this list reports human genetic association between ZBED5 variants and blood glucose, nor any expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence connecting ZBED5 to glucose homeostasis. The co-mention is incidental and provides no logical biological basis for a link. Accordingly, the evidence supports a Novel classification, with only minimal probability retained for hypothesized biology not represented in this corpus.

None of the provided articles address varicose veins or venous insufficiency in any form. The literature on DEFB104A (and the copy-number variable 8p23.1 beta-defensin cluster including DEFB4/DEFB103/DEFB104) concerns psoriasis, Crohn's disease, HIV susceptibility, dermatophytosis, prostate cancer, pancreatitis, SLE/vasculitis, and ischemic stroke — none of which are recognized precursors, subtypes, or mechanisms of varicose veins. The single vascular-related paper (ischemic stroke, PMID 22050386) concerns arterial thrombotic disease and DEFB1/DEFB4, not varicose veins, and provides no logical bridge. At most, a weak, generic inflammation/innate-immunity rationale could be invoked, which supports only a small allowance for "Hypothesized." No human variant evidence links DEFB104A to varicose veins, so "Established" is excluded.

All retrieved articles concern POPDC1/BVES in striated muscle biology, cardiac pacemaking/conduction, limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type R25 with atrioventricular block, and tumor suppression; none address peripheral artery disease (PAD) or any vascular occlusive/ischemic limb phenotype. No human genetic study here reports POPDC1 variants associated with PAD, so Established and Existing cannot be supported. A small residual weight is given to Hypothesized because POPDC1 is named "blood vessel epicardial substance" and is implicated in endothelial/epithelial junction and cell migration biology, and because LGMDR25 causes lower-limb weakness that could superficially be confused with claudication—but these are indirect and not evidence of a PAD link. The overwhelming likelihood is that co-mention is incidental, supporting the Novel category.

All retrieved articles concern SPRN (Shadoo, shadow of prion protein) in the context of transmissible spongiform encephalopathies — scrapie, BSE, CJD — across humans, sheep, goats, cattle, horses, rabbits, ducks, pheasants, and mice. None of the abstracts mention kidney function, renal disease, nephropathy, or any phenotype related to chronic renal failure. There is no biological pathway, expression, or animal-model evidence in this literature connecting SPRN to renal pathology. The gene–phenotype pairing appears entirely incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

None of the provided articles measure or report alanine transaminase (ALT) or any liver-enzyme phenotype. NBEAL1 variants in humans are reported in relation to coronary artery disease, cerebral small vessel disease/intracerebral haemorrhage, and BMI/anorexia nervosa (PMIDs 32161285, 31430377, 27184124), with no proband, family, or cohort evidence linking NBEAL1 variants to ALT levels, so Established and Existing cannot be supported. A modest allowance for Hypothesized is warranted because NBEAL1 regulates SREBP2 processing, LDLR expression, and cholesterol metabolism (PMID 32161285), pathways central to hepatic lipid handling and steatosis, which is a recognized determinant of circulating ALT. The remaining literature (BDCP structural work, Neurobeachin in hematopoiesis, long-read SV mapping in neurodegeneration) is unrelated to ALT and constitutes incidental co-mention. Overall the evidence base is best described as Novel with some biologically plausible, indirect mechanistic rationale.

Only one human genetic-variant study directly tests BMP1 variation against HDL: PMID 30062502 reports that the BMP1 5'UTR +104 T/C (rs143383) genotype associates with serum ApoA1 and HDL-C in male controls (with no effect in statin-treated CHD patients), a small single-cohort study without replication. Supporting but non-variant human data include PMID 30430582, where BMP1 transcript levels in mononuclear cells differ between hyper- and hypoalphalipoproteinemic subjects. Strong mechanistic biology exists—BMP1 cleaves proapoA1 to its phospholipid-binding form (PMID 17580958)—and PCPE2, the BMP1 enhancer, affects HDL in mice (PMID 25947382), but these are in vitro/animal and support only Hypothesized. Because I cannot cite two independent human variant studies with their own positive results, Established is unlikely; the bulk of the remaining BMP1 literature concerns osteogenesis imperfecta and is irrelevant to HDL.

None of the provided articles report any genetic variant, association, or functional link between CPNE2 and type 2 diabetes. The copine papers (PMIDs 26175110, 9430674) describe calcium-dependent phospholipid binding and membrane trafficking biology with no diabetes phenotype, and the glioblastoma study (PMID 36979157) mentions CPNE2 only in the context of EGFR surface abundance in tumor cells. The one diabetes-related paper (PMID 36115450) concerns type 1 diabetes serum proteomics and refers to "CPN2" (carboxypeptidase N subunit 2), a homonymous acronym, not CPNE2. Therefore the evidence base is incidental co-mention at best, supporting a Novel classification, with a small allowance for hypothesized calcium-signaling/membrane-trafficking relevance to insulin secretion.

phenotype: Waist to hip ratio adjusted for BMI
justification: None of the provided articles address waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI, adiposity, fat distribution, or any metabolic/anthropometric trait. The papers concern ZNF283 methylation-expression relationships in high-grade serous ovarian cancer, an antiviral role against PRRSV in porcine cells, and differential expression during FMDV infection in a pig kidney cell line — the latter two being non-human, in vitro studies. There is no human genetic variant evidence linking ZNF283 to WHRadjBMI, nor any biological pathway plausibly connecting the KRAB zinc-finger transcriptional repressor function described here to body fat distribution. The co-mentions are incidental, supporting a Novel classification, with only a small residual probability that GWAS evidence exists outside this article set.

None of the provided articles report any association between TNFSF15 variants and hematocrit or any red blood cell/erythrocyte trait. The literature is dominated by TNFSF15/TL1A associations with inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis), psoriasis, IgA nephropathy, primary biliary cirrhosis, and leprosy reactions, plus functional immunology of TL1A–DR3 signaling in lymphocytes and murine ileitis. A tenuous indirect argument could be made that chronic intestinal inflammation and blood loss in IBD alters hematocrit, giving minimal weight to "Hypothesized," but no paper measures or models hematocrit. There is no human genetic evidence tying TNFSF15 variants to hematocrit, so "Established" and "Existing" are essentially unsupported.

None of the provided articles report any association between WDR59 variants and diastolic blood pressure or hypertension. The closest human genetic evidence is an exome-wide association study in UK Biobank linking WDR59 to snoring (PMID 38177695); sleep-disordered breathing is a recognized risk factor for elevated blood pressure, which provides indirect, non-definitive support for the "Existing" category. Additional human evidence links biallelic WDR59 variants to syndromic dilated cardiomyopathy (PMID 41715954), a cardiac phenotype but not a blood-pressure trait per se, though it does implicate GATOR2–mTORC1 signaling in cardiovascular homeostasis, supporting a plausible biological (hypothesized) link. The remaining papers (PMIDs 23723238, 38372438, 36444289, 27173016) are in vitro/structural or epilepsy-focused studies of GATOR complexes with no relevance to blood pressure. Overall the evidence is largely incidental, so weight is concentrated on Novel/Hypothesized with modest support for Existing.

HDLC refers to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, but none of the retrieved articles address lipid traits, cholesterol metabolism, or cardiovascular/metabolic phenotypes. Every paper concerns SYCP1 as a synaptonemal complex component in meiosis, spermatogenesis, infertility/azoospermia, follicular assembly, litter size, or testicular germ-cell tumor epigenetics. There is no biological pathway, expression, or animal-model evidence linking SYCP1 to HDL cholesterol in this corpus; the one GWAS-like study (intracranial aneurysm linkage) is unrelated to lipids. Therefore the gene–phenotype relationship is best described as Novel, with only a small allowance for a hypothesized link that is not supported here.

phenotype: Lump or mass in breast or nonspecific abnormal breast exam
justification: The strongest breast-related evidence is a human immunohistochemical/expression study reporting REPS2 as a favourable prognostic and predictive biomarker in breast cancer (PMID 19776672), reiterated as background in a review (PMID 21907823) and in an esophageal cancer study (PMID 23803043); these are protein-expression and functional data, not analyses of genetic variants, so they support a biologically plausible link rather than a variant-based association. No article reports REPS2 sequence variants in probands, families, or cohorts with breast lumps/masses; the only germline findings are multigene Xp22 microdeletions/duplications in Nance-Horan syndrome and X-linked intellectual disability (PMIDs 20882036, 20613765), which cannot implicate REPS2 specifically and concern unrelated phenotypes. Other papers involve Drosophila/mouse models or in silico work (PMIDs 39271109, 38766038, 15081118, 15010845), which cannot elevate the evidence beyond Hypothesized. Therefore Hypothesized carries most weight, with modest probability for Existing given the human tumour-tissue biomarker data.

None of the provided articles mention cervical cancer or any oncologic phenotype. All IFT140 literature here concerns ciliopathies: retinal dystrophy, Mainzer-Saldino/Jeune/Sensenbrenner syndromes, polycystic kidney disease, nephronophthisis, spermatogenic dysfunction, and hypothalamic hamartoma. There is no genetic, functional, expression, or animal-model evidence linking IFT140 variation to cervical carcinogenesis or to a recognized precursor such as HPV-related cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. Therefore the gene–disease relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a negligible possibility that generic ciliary/Hedgehog signaling biology could provide a speculative hypothesized link.

No article in this set reports human genetic variants in KRT79 associated with a "protein" phenotype (e.g., protein levels/pQTL); the CNV study in beef cattle (PMID 37959106) is non-human and involves a multi-gene duplication spanning KRT4/KRT78/KRT79, which cannot implicate KRT79 specifically. The strongest mechanistic support is biological: KRT79 encodes a type II cytokeratin structural protein with documented expression and functional roles in hair follicle, sebaceous/meibomian gland, and liver (PPARA-regulated) biology, largely from mouse models (PMIDs 36796223, 31564613, 41850650, 27672671). Human-derived data are limited to in vitro proteomic detection of KRT79 among differentially expressed proteins in A549 lung cancer cells (PMID 27573346) and transcriptomic/computational gene-selection in eosinophilic esophagitis (PMID 39643769), neither of which involves genetic variants. This pattern — direct protein-level and functional relevance without human variant evidence — fits "Hypothesized" best, with residual probability for "Novel" given the vagueness of the phenotype and for "Existing" given the human expression/proteomic reports.

None of the provided articles mention hypothyroidism or thyroid function in any capacity. MRGPRX4 literature focuses exclusively on cholestatic/jaundice-associated pruritus (bile acid and bilirubin receptor biology), menthol cigarette smoking preference, melanoma oncogenic signaling, and pharmacological agonist/antagonist development. There are no human genetic association studies, animal models, or mechanistic pathways linking MRGPRX4 variation or biology to thyroid hormone deficiency. The only tangential connections are shared contexts of liver disease and bile acid receptor signaling, which do not provide a logical basis for a hypothyroidism link. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

All retrieved articles concern SPO11's canonical role in initiating meiotic DNA double-strand breaks, homologous recombination, chromosome segregation, and male infertility in yeast, mouse, fungi, and human infertility cohorts. None measure monocyte percentage or any hematologic/immune trait, and no biological pathway linking SPO11 to monocyte biology is described. Human genetic studies cited (e.g., SPO11 C631T and male infertility) address a reproductive phenotype unrelated to blood cell counts. There is therefore no direct, indirect, or mechanistic evidence connecting SPO11 variants to monocyte percentage; the co-mentions would be incidental.

All three provided articles concern SPATS1 in the context of spermatogenesis and gonadal development (mouse knockout, fish gonad transcriptomics, turtle DKKL1 study), and none measure or mention gamma-glutamyl transferase or any liver/metabolic phenotype. No human genetic association study, variant, or cohort linking SPATS1 to GGT levels appears in the list. There is also no plausible biological pathway articulated in these papers connecting SPATS1 to hepatic enzyme levels, so even a "hypothesized" designation lacks support. The evidence base is therefore consistent with an incidental co-mention or no relationship at all.

The only human genetic work directly touching alcohol phenotypes is the candidate-gene study of adenylyl cyclase genes (ADCY1-9) in alcohol dependence with comorbid depression (PMID 23278386) and the Framingham gene–alcohol interaction GWAS, where ADCY2 appeared among suggestive loci for SNP-by-alcohol-consumption interaction on blood pressure (PMID 24376456). Neither provides a robust, replicated primary association between ADCY2 variants and alcohol consumption itself; the interaction study's phenotype is blood pressure, and the candidate-gene study focuses on alcoholism/depression comorbidity across the whole ADCY family. The bulk of remaining ADCY2 literature concerns bipolar disorder (PMIDs 24618891, 32447269, 39003412), cancer, cardiac CNVs, and cAMP biology, which supply mechanistic plausibility (cAMP signaling in reward and mood, animal/in vitro data) rather than alcohol-consumption genetics. Hence "Existing" is the most probable label, with substantial weight on "Hypothesized" given the largely indirect/mechanistic nature of the evidence; "Established" cannot be supported because two independent human cohorts reporting ADCY2 variants associated with alcohol consumption cannot be cited.

None of the provided articles report any genetic variant in SEMA6D associated with essential hypertension or blood pressure traits; the human genetic studies concern COVID-19 susceptibility, Behçet's disease, smoking behaviour, ADHD/obesity, language impairment, and APOE-related cognition. Indirect biological plausibility exists: Sema6D/Plexin-A1 signalling regulates cardiac morphogenesis and interacts with VEGFR2 in angiogenesis (PMIDs 14977921, 27895757), and endothelial Sema6D controls sympathetic innervation (PMID 41729164), a pathway relevant to blood pressure regulation — but these are murine/chick/in vitro data with no hypertension phenotype measured. Therefore Established and Existing are effectively excluded, and the weight lies between Novel (no evidence of a hypertension link) and Hypothesized (vascular/sympathetic biology offering a mechanistic rationale).

The evidence linking LGR6 to alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is entirely functional and non-human: Lgr6-null mice show reduced ALP activity in periosteal progenitors and impaired osteogenesis (PMID 36708855), BMP9 upregulates LGR6 to increase ALP expression/activity in MC3T3-E1 murine osteoblastic cells (PMID 31914211), and LGR6 knockdown modulates osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs (PMID 29625528). These establish a plausible biological mechanism (Wnt/β-catenin–mediated osteoblast differentiation with ALP as a readout) but involve no human variant data on ALP levels. The only human genetic study (PMID 34795657) associates LGR6 rs10920362 with osteoporosis/BMD and gut microbiota, not with alkaline phosphatase measurements, so it cannot support Established or clearly support Existing. No article reports human variants in LGR6 associated with serum/tissue ALP, so Hypothesized is the best fit.

None of the provided articles address bacteremia, sepsis, or SIRS in any form. The STX6 literature here concerns neurodegenerative disease genetics (progressive supranuclear palsy, sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, FTLD) and basic cell-biological roles of syntaxin-6 in SNARE-mediated intracellular vesicle trafficking (Golgi/TGN transport, GLUT4 and TRPV5 trafficking, dense core vesicle biogenesis). No human genetic association, expression, or functional study links STX6 variation or activity to systemic infection or inflammatory response phenotypes. The only conceivable connection would be a generic role of SNARE proteins in secretory/immune cell function, which is not demonstrated in any of these papers, so the co-mentions are effectively absent rather than merely incidental.

Neither article addresses hemoglobin concentration or any erythrocyte/hematological trait. PMID 34884508 is an in vitro glioblastoma study of GRPEL2 in mitochondrial redox regulation, and PMID 35548910 reports DNA methylation changes (not genetic variants) in vinyl chloride-exposed workers, with GRPEL2 as one of many differentially methylated genes unrelated to hemoglobin levels. There are no human genetic association data, GWAS findings, or phenotype measurements of blood hemoglobin for GRPEL2 in the provided literature. A small allowance is given to "Hypothesized" because GRPEL2's role in mitochondrial protein import and redox homeostasis is loosely relevant to erythroid mitochondrial biology, but the co-mentions here are essentially incidental.

None of the provided articles mention C-reactive protein, inflammation biomarkers, or any acute-phase response phenotype. All papers concern SMG5 as a component of the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay machinery, with functions in spermatogenesis, oligodendrocyte differentiation, cancer prognosis, viral RNA regulation, and a rare developmental delay syndrome. The only human variant study (PMID 41758221) describes a homozygous synonymous SMG5 variant causing developmental delay and growth retardation, with no link to CRP levels. There is no genetic, expression, or pathway evidence connecting SMG5 to C-reactive protein, so the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for indirect biological plausibility via general transcriptome regulation.

None of the provided articles addresses rheumatic heart disease, streptococcal autoimmunity, or valvular pathology; the literature is dominated by GPR17 biology in oligodendrocyte precursor differentiation, remyelination, CNS injury, glioma, and schizophrenia (e.g., PMID 40011789, 32086854, 39703181). The only cardiac-relevant study concerns GPR17-expressing stromal/mesenchymal cell trafficking after murine myocardial infarction (PMID 24909956), which involves ischemic rather than rheumatic heart disease and is in animals/in vitro. Broad reviews of orphan GPCRs in ischemia (PMID 38906238) similarly provide no link to rheumatic heart disease. There are no human genetic variant studies connecting GPR17 to this phenotype, so Established and Existing cannot be supported. A small amount of weight is given to Hypothesized because GPR17 is a cysteinyl-leukotriene/nucleotide receptor with inflammatory and cardiac-cell functions, offering a tenuous biological rationale.

There are several human case-control genetic association studies specifically examining PPARA variants and breast cancer risk: the Long Island population-based study reported a doubling of risk for rs4253760 homozygotes (PMID 18586686), a Taiwanese study reported combined PPARA/APOE polymorphism effects on breast cancer risk (PMID 23076161), and a Chinese Han study examined PPARA–PPARG gene–gene interaction on breast cancer risk (PMID 28669518). These are association-level findings in humans, with the original authors themselves calling for independent replication, and they do not demonstrate causality in probands or families. Most other listed papers concern PPARG/PPARγ polymorphisms or generic PPAR pathway signatures, which do not constitute PPARA-specific variant evidence. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit; "Established" is not supported since no two studies demonstrate a replicated causal role, and "Hypothesized" retains modest weight given some evidence is only pathway-level.

None of the provided articles mention asthma (or asthenia) at all; the human genetic evidence for DDX39B concerns multiple sclerosis risk via IL7R exon 6 splicing (PMID 28340352) and a neurodevelopmental syndrome (PMIDs 39918047, 40651286), not Asth. Therefore no article can be cited as demonstrating causal or associated variants in Asth patients, ruling out Established and largely ruling out Existing. Some indirect biological plausibility exists because DDX39B is an MHC class III–region immune regulator that controls FOXP3/Treg differentiation, IL7R soluble receptor production, and NF-κB inflammatory signalling (PMIDs 38575347, 41615953, 32209106), pathways broadly relevant to allergic/inflammatory airway disease, which supports partial weight on Hypothesized. However, since the link is entirely inferential and asthma is never assessed, the majority of the probability rests on Novel.

None of the provided articles measure bilirubin or address hepatic/heme metabolism. The literature concerns WASHC2C (FAM21) in retromer/WASH-mediated endosomal sorting, NF-κB regulation in pancreatic cancer cells, TBC1D23-related pontocerebellar hypoplasia, ALS-FTD gene screening, and an imaging-genetics study of reward system reactivity. Human genetic studies cited involve neurological phenotypes, not bilirubin levels, so they cannot support Established or Existing. A weak biological rationale (endosomal receptor recycling could theoretically affect hepatic transporter trafficking) is speculative and not stated in any abstract, so only minimal weight is given to Hypothesized.

Multiple human case-control studies report associations between AHR variants (notably Arg554Lys/rs2066853) and breast cancer risk or prognosis: the Shanghai Breast Cancer Study (PMID 16538170), its stage-2 evaluation (PMID 21454829), a Thai study (PMID 19415745), an Egyptian prognostic study (PMID 38615265), and Swedish cohort analyses of AHR genotype with outcome (PMIDs 34094928, 40646277). However, evidence is inconsistent — a large multiethnic cohort (PMID 16103451) and a meta-analysis (PMID 26662408) found no association — so the relationship is associative and unresolved rather than causal, precluding "Established." Supporting biology (AhR overexpression in triple-negative disease, macrophage AhR in metastatic niche, dietary ligands) reinforces plausibility but is largely mechanistic/animal-based (PMIDs 39690159, 29962921, 26715507), which supports "Hypothesized" rather than genetic causation. No study demonstrates rare pathogenic AHR variants segregating in independent probands/families, so Established receives minimal weight.
